candidate_seeds.stem:
If v(t)=3t², the acceleration at t=2 s is

A. 3 m/s²
B. 6 m/s²
C. 12 m/s²
D. 24 m/s²

choices.rationale: Mistakes the leading coefficient 3 in v(t)=3t² for the acceleration itself, as in the x=½at² form.

Mistakenly differentiates v(t)=3t² using an incomplete power rule (dropping the exponent multiplier), computing dv/dt=3t instead of the correct 6t, then evaluates 3(2)=6 m/s² at the correct time t=2 s.
dv/dt=6t, evaluated at t=2 s gives 12 m/s².
Multiplies 6t by t again instead of substituting t=2, giving 6t²=6(2)²=24.

candidate_seeds.stem:
The displacement from t=0 to T for v(t)=kt is

A. kT
B. kT²
C. kT²/2
D. k/T

choices.rationale: Uses the final velocity v(T)=kT times T instead of integrating the linearly increasing velocity, skipping the 1/2 averaging factor.
Integrates kt dt to kT² but drops the 1/2 factor that comes from the power rule.
integrating kt gives kT²/2
Divides the acceleration constant k by T instead of integrating velocity over time, confusing acceleration units with displacement.

candidate_seeds.stem:
A force F(x)=ax acts in one dimension. The work from 0 to L is

A. aL
B. aL²
C. aL²/2
D. a/L

choices.rationale: Mistakes the endpoint force value F(L)=aL for the work itself, without multiplying by the displacement.
Multiplies the endpoint force F(L)=aL by the full distance L as if the force were constant, missing the 1/2 factor from integrating the linearly increasing force.
the integral of ax dx is aL²/2
Divides the force gradient a by L, confusing the differential relationship dF/dx=a with the work integral.

candidate_seeds.stem:
A particle moves in one dimension under a conservative force with potential energy U(x). The force on the particle is given by which of the following?

A. dU/dx
B. -dU/dx
C. -U/x
D. +d^2U/dx^2

choices.rationale: Drops the negative sign, forgetting that force opposes (rather than follows) the direction of increasing potential energy.
force is the negative potential gradient
This has the correct sign but treats the relationship as simple division rather than differentiation, as though U were directly proportional to x -- it agrees with -dU/dx only in that special case.
This differentiates U twice and drops the sign. The second derivative describes how steeply the force itself changes with position (related to the stiffness of the potential well), not the force.

candidate_seeds.stem:
A power law P(t)=ct² delivers energy from 0 to T equal to

A. cT²
B. cT³/2
C. cT³/3
D. 2cT

choices.rationale: Evaluates the power at time T and treats that instantaneous value as the total energy, without integrating over the interval.
Integrates ct² correctly in form but uses the wrong power-rule denominator, writing t³/2 instead of t³/3.
energy is the time integral of power
Differentiates P(t)=ct² instead of integrating it, computing d/dt(ct²)=2ct and evaluating at T.

candidate_seeds.stem:
At a stable equilibrium x₀, U(x) has

A. a local minimum
B. a local maximum
C. an infinite slope
D. no derivative

choices.rationale: small displacements raise potential energy
Confuses stable equilibrium with unstable equilibrium, where the potential sits at a local maximum instead.
Assumes equilibrium requires the slope to blow up rather than vanish, misreading dU/dx=0 as an undefined or infinite condition.
Assumes equilibrium points must be non-smooth kinks in U(x) rather than smooth minima where dU/dx=0.

candidate_seeds.stem:
Torque from potential energy U(θ), for a system whose potential energy depends only on the angle θ, is

A. dU/dθ
B. -dU/dθ
C. -U/θ
D. +d²U/dθ²

choices.rationale: Drops the negative sign, forgetting that torque opposes the direction of increasing potential energy.
generalized force is minus the potential derivative
Incorrect. Treats torque as the total potential energy divided by the angle (a ratio), rather than as the instantaneous rate of change of potential energy with angle (a derivative).

Incorrect. This is the second derivative of U with respect to θ (related to the curvature/stiffness of the potential, as appears in small-angle oscillation problems), not the first derivative that defines torque.

candidate_seeds.stem:
If x(t)=At³-Bt, velocity is

A. 3At²-B
B. At²-B
C. 3At-B
D. A t³

choices.rationale: differentiate position with respect to time
Drops the coefficient 3 that the power rule brings down from At³, reducing the exponent without multiplying by it.
Reduces the exponent on At³ by one too many, an off-by-one power-rule slip giving t instead of t².
Forgets to differentiate the At³ term at all and drops the -Bt term entirely, leaving the position expression unchanged.

candidate_seeds.stem:
A force F(x)=F₀e^{-x/L} acts along the direction of displacement, with L a positive constant. The work done as the object moves from x=0 to x→∞ is

A. F₀/L
B. F₀L
C. zero
D. infinite

choices.rationale: Inverts the decay length, dividing by L instead of multiplying, as if the integral shrank rather than scaled by the decay length.
The integral ∫₀^∞ F₀e^{-x/L}dx = F₀L converges because L>0 makes the exponential decay (not grow) as x increases.
Assumes the force decaying to zero as x→∞ means the enclosed area (work) also vanishes, rather than converging to a finite nonzero value.
Assumes an infinite integration limit must always produce infinite work, missing that the exponential integrand decays fast enough to converge.

candidate_seeds.stem:
For τ(t)=τ₀t acting on constant I, change in angular speed from 0 to T is

A. τ₀T/I
B. τ₀T²/(2I)
C. Iτ₀T²
D. τ₀T²/I

choices.rationale: This applies the constant-torque impulse formula Δω=τT/I using τ0 as if it were the full (constant) torque magnitude, rather than recognizing τ(t)=τ0t is linearly increasing -- τ0 here is only a proportionality constant, not the torque itself -- so integration is required, introducing the T² (not T) time dependence.
Integrating α=τ(t)/I=τ0t/I over time from 0 to T gives Δω=τ0T²/(2I).
Multiplies by I instead of dividing by it, inverting where the moment of inertia belongs in α=τ/I.
Integrates in the correct form but omits the 1/2 factor that comes from integrating t dt.

C. g/I
D. mgI/d

choices.rationale: linearizing Iθ''=-mgdθ gives ω²=mgd/I
Inverts the correct ratio, swapping the numerator and denominator of mgd/I.
Drops the mass m and pivot distance d from the numerator, misapplying the simple pendulum's g/L form instead of adapting for the physical pendulum's torque equation.
Multiplies by I instead of dividing by it, inverting where the moment of inertia belongs in the ratio.

This takes a third derivative and therefore gives jerk.

candidate_seeds.stem:
The signed area under a velocity-versus-time graph equals

A. acceleration
B. displacement
C. distance traveled
D. change in velocity

choices.rationale: Acceleration is the slope of velocity versus time, not its area.
The time integral of velocity is the signed change in position.
Distance traveled adds all areas as positive, but signed velocity-time area gives displacement.
Change in velocity comes from integrating acceleration, not velocity.

candidate_seeds.stem:

choices.rationale: This ignores the incline angle and uses the full weight.

Frictionless means no frictional force; the incline still exerts a normal force.

candidate_seeds.stem:

candidate_seeds.stem:

D. neither total energy nor momentum is conserved

choices.choice_text: momentum and kinetic energy are conserved
choices.rationale: This incorrectly treats sticking as an elastic interaction.

choices.choice_text: momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not

choices.rationale: This reverses the two conservation results.

choices.choice_text: neither total energy nor momentum is conserved
